prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength enable frequency standards of unprecedented accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: I keep B041 as my single-part position. The achievement is a specific scheme: trapping many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength so that the lattice light shift cancels on the clock transition. It was then taken to roughly 1e-18 fractional uncertainty, about two orders of magnitude beyond caesium. The accuracy is credible because the atomic-structure side was controlled quantitatively: the magic wavelength itself, blackbody radiation, hyperfine and higher-order light shifts, and collisional shifts. Several independent laboratories now agree at this level, and the result supports the roadmap for redefining the second, tests of fundamental constants and dark-matter models, and relativistic geodesy. The credit is the cleanest on the shortlist: Katori for the concept and first realisation, Ye for the accuracy and stability record and the many-body clock. Having read the whole first round, I take Pearce's point and have tightened the citation so that it names the neutral-atom lattice scheme rather than clocks in general. That wording is the answer to the 2012 ion-control prize as well as the 2005 comb prize. Broad support for B046 is not evidence against B041, and the support counts do not decide it for me; the question is which achievement is more mature, better attributed and distinct from earlier prizes.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged: a colleague outside atomic physics could read B041 as refinement of lines already honoured in 2005 (frequency comb) and 2012 (single-ion control), and the redefinition of the second, the most visible consequence, has not yet happened. Strontium, ytterbium and aluminium-ion clock groups in Paris, Boulder, Braunschweig and elsewhere contributed to the systematic-uncertainty work, and a two-name prize cannot represent them. Priority for the magic-wavelength idea is shared among several proposers, which I am recalling from memory. B046 has the broadest opening support, and Eriksson, Kroll and Danielsson argue persuasively that opening a new class of correlated materials is a larger scientific event than a further order of magnitude in clock accuracy. I do not dismiss that. My view is only that B046 is younger and its attribution is harder to defend, and that the committee can reasonably choose either.

responses.point: Eriksson moved B046 above his opening first choice, calling it the cleanest prediction-then-discovery chain on the shortlist, and judges the 2011 flat-band prediction and the 2018 observation to map onto the credited trio.
responses.response: The prediction-then-observation chain is real, and I do not contest that the 2018 result is secure. What I cannot get past is that the mapping onto three names is not clean. The experimental side rests on Jarillo-Herrero, while Cao as first author and the Dean, Yacoby and Young groups, who established the phenomenology independently, are outside the credit, and you propose to cover that by wording the citation around the group. A citation can say 'group', but the prize names people. Your own comparison, that B001 would be better established on maturity, makes the same point I would make for B041 against B046: when the pairing mechanism is still open, the committee is recognising a platform before it knows what the physics is. I also disagree that clock accuracy is a mere refinement. The lattice clock changes what is measurable and was understood at the level of individual shifts, which is the same theory-experiment closure you value in B046.

responses.point: Danielsson holds that the 2011 prediction and 2018 discovery created a field with many independent groups and platforms, and that the unsettled pairing mechanism does not bar recognition, since the prize would honour the flat-band prediction and observed phases.
responses.response: I accept the distinction between honouring the discovery and honouring a solved mechanism, and it moves me a little: I no longer treat the open pairing mechanism as a strong objection in itself. My remaining difficulty is sample dependence and the experimental credit. You say twist-angle disorder makes reproducibility uneven, and you also say the three-name split maps neatly onto theory and experiment. Both cannot be fully comfortable at once, because the independent confirmations come from groups that are not credited. For B041 the independent agreement is between clocks of different species and different laboratories, and it is a quantitative agreement at the 1e-18 level, which is a stronger form of reproduction. I keep B046 as my first alternative and I would not call a B046 prize wrong.

responses.point: Kroll's round-1 case against B041 raises the overlap with the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, notes that the second has not been redefined, and discloses a research stay in John Hall's laboratory, from which Jun Ye descends scientifically.
responses.response: I share your reading of the overlap risk and my citation now responds to it explicitly. The comb counts optical cycles, the ion prize concerned single trapped quantum systems, and the lattice clock combines a new reference, a large ensemble with the light shift cancelled, with the performance that follows from it. On recusal, from my side a mentor link to the JILA environment, with no joint work with Katori or Ye, seems to me a disclosure matter and not a reason to step back, but I would defer to the chair. I note that because three of the eight members support B041, a recusal would shift the balance, and I would want that settled openly, not left to the ballot.

responses.point: Pearce moved to B041 from his IceCube first choice, asks that the citation make explicit that the recognised achievement is the neutral-atom lattice scheme and its 1e-18 performance and not clocks in general, and says the Yb and Al+ groups add pressure on the two-name credit.
responses.response: I adopted your wording request, and the citation now says the optical lattice clock with neutral atoms at a magic wavelength. On the other groups, I do not think the two names are arbitrary: Katori made the concept and first realisation, and Ye's group set the accuracy and stability record that made the clock a candidate for the second. The Al+ ion clocks belong to a different scheme, which is itself why the 2012 prize does not cover B041. The strontium and ytterbium groups in Paris, PTB and Boulder who reproduced and extended the results are the real attribution pressure, and I do not claim it is zero. I would still say a two-name prize is defensible, because the committee credits the originator and the person who showed the concept reaches its limit.

responses.point: Johansson judges B046 secure as a discovery even if its microscopic explanation is not, notes that a colleague who weights maturity heavily can fairly resist, and states that B041 and B046 do not compete for the same slot across years.
responses.response: I agree that the two ballots are not mutually exclusive over time, and I would be content with B046 later. I am less convinced by the argument that B041's support is too concentrated: six members ranked it and all of them proposed the same two names, which counts for coherence of the credit. You are also right that I am the member most likely to be counted as a maturity-minded colleague here. I do prefer the older, better-attributed achievement. But I want to be honest that I would not argue a B046 prize is premature on scientific grounds, only that the experimental credit is awkward.

responses.point: Mehlig keeps dynamical mean-field theory (B001) as his lead, citing thirty years of confirmation and conceptual originality, and acknowledges that Metzner is outside the credit and that B001 is arguably a method and not a discovery of nature.
responses.response: I agree with you that long confirmation is the strongest criterion and that B001 scores well on it, and I treat your attribution doubt about Metzner as serious. My difficulty with B001 is the one you state yourself: the credited trio does not match the history of the infinite-dimension limit, and as an atomic theorist I can judge neither the impurity mapping nor the history of the Mott transition picture well enough to rank it above B041. On the maturity argument you and I point the same way, and it is the main reason I place B041 ahead of B046. I would resist moving B001 above both on the strength of maturity alone while the three-name credit is still open.

uncertainties: Whether the committee wants to wait for the formal redefinition of the SI second, or considers demonstrated performance sufficient; I lean towards the latter.
Whether the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes make B041 read as incremental to colleagues outside atomic physics; the revised citation tries to address this but cannot remove it.
Priority for the magic-wavelength idea and the weight of other strontium, ytterbium and ion-clock groups, which I am recalling from memory and have not verified.

Whether B046 would be judged more significant by the committee, since its supporters reasonably weigh a new field above a refined technique; I cannot rule this out and would accept it as a defensible outcome.
Whether a two-part configuration is defensible; I still find no pairing that works on attribution within three names.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B041 (Katori, Ye) or the alternatives B046 and B038, and I have no joint work with Katori or Ye. I repeat my broader disclosure as an atomic theorist: a long-running collaboration with Anne L'Huillier, papers with the Lund group and Ursula Keller's group at ETH, and work with Reinhold Schuch and others. None of these people is a credited name in my configuration, and such ties would require recusal only on an attosecond candidate, which is not on the shortlist. I note Kroll's disclosure on B041 and regard it as a matter for open disclosure.
